text:
Park the Mandate: Why Cities Should Scrap Minimum Parking Requirements

Walk through almost any American city and you will find a quiet rule shaping the ground beneath your feet. Before a single apartment, restaurant, or clinic can be built, the planning code says how many parking spaces must come with it. Often the number is startling. A restaurant might need one space for every hundred square feet of dining room. An apartment building might need two spaces per unit, regardless of whether the tenants own cars. These minimum parking requirements are among the most consequential and least debated rules in urban policy. Cities should abolish them.

Start with the origin of the rules, because it is humbling. Most minimums were not carefully derived from local conditions. Planners in the mid twentieth century leaned on a handbook of parking generation rates, which compiled surveys of mostly suburban sites with free, abundant parking. The numbers reflected the peak demand at those places on their busiest days, then became law. A city copied its neighbor, the neighbor copied the handbook, and the guesswork hardened into code. No one ever proved that the right amount of parking is whatever it takes to make a lot nearly empty on the busiest day of the year.

The consequences of this guesswork are large. Parking is expensive to build. A surface space consumes roughly three hundred square feet once you count the aisles, and land is the most valuable thing a city has. A space in a structure can cost tens of thousands of dollars, and underground spaces cost far more. Those costs do not vanish. They are passed on through higher rents, higher menu prices, and higher prices for everything sold in a building that must subsidize its own storage for cars. Worse, the cost lands on everyone equally, including the household that owns no car at all. Requiring parking is a tax on people who do not drive, collected to benefit people who do.

It also kills housing and businesses that would otherwise exist. Consider a small lot downtown where a developer wants to build twelve modest apartments. If the code demands twenty four spaces, the math collapses. Either the project shrinks, the project becomes a pricier product aimed at wealthier buyers, or it never happens. Older neighborhoods are full of charming corner shops and small apartment buildings that could not legally be built today, because their lots are too small to hold the required asphalt. Minimums effectively outlaw the kind of dense, walkable, affordable places that people pay a premium to live in.

Consider what cities look like when the rules take over. Large stretches of downtowns in places that mandated parking have been hollowed into parking lots and garages, with buildings spaced far apart and sidewalks that lead nowhere. Walking becomes unpleasant because the distances grow and the destinations thin out. That in turn makes driving feel mandatory, which creates the demand for more parking. The rule produces the very problem it claims to solve.

Defenders raise honest objections. They worry that without requirements, new buildings will flood the neighborhood with cars competing for street spots. This fear deserves a direct answer. First, developers are not fools. Lenders and builders know that many tenants want a space, and they will keep building parking where the market wants it. The difference is that the number would come from demand, not from a formula. Buildings near transit might offer fewer spaces and cheaper rent. Buildings in car oriented areas would still include plenty. Second, the street parking problem is really a pricing problem. Curb space is valuable, and cities that give it away for free will always have shortages. Charging fair rates for curb parking, or giving residents permits, manages spillover far better than forcing every building to overbuild.

The evidence from places that have tried reform is encouraging. Buffalo, New York, eliminated citywide minimums in 2017 and saw developers build projects with parking tailored to their sites, while the sky did not fall. Minneapolis, Portland, and a growing list of other cities have scaled back or abolished requirements. Developers there frequently still build parking, but they build less of it, and they build it where it serves actual customers. Studies of reforms have found that when the mandate lifts, builders tend to supply fewer spaces than the code once demanded, which tells us the old numbers were inflated.

There is a climate and fairness argument too. Transportation is a leading source of greenhouse gas emissions in many countries, and abundant free parking is a standing invitation to drive for every trip. Removing the mandate does not ban cars. It simply stops forcing cities to prefer them. It also helps households of modest means, who are more likely to rely on transit and who bear the burden of paying for spaces they never use.

Abolishing minimums is not an attack on drivers. It is a return to common sense. Let property owners, lenders, and tenants decide how much parking a building needs, just as they decide how many bathrooms or elevators it needs. Where parking is truly valuable, it will be provided and priced honestly. Where it is not, land can go to homes, shops, and trees. A city that insists on counting spaces before it counts people has its priorities backward. It is time to park the mandate for good.
